definition: Criminal procedure deals with the set of rules governing the series of proceedings through which the government enforces substantive criminal law. Municipalities, states, and the federal government all have their own criminal codes, defining types of conduct that constitute crimes. Title 18 of the U.S. Code outlines the majority of federal crimes and criminal procedure. Typically, federal crimes deal with activities that either extend beyond state boundaries or directly impact federal interests. Federal Federal prosecutions follow the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, also cited as Fed. R. Crim. P., which the U.S. Supreme Court promulgated. The Federal Rules outline the procedure for conducting federal criminal trials and incorporate and expound upon all guarantees included within the U.S. Constitution's Bill of Rights, such as the guarantee to due process, the right to legal counsel, the right to confront witnesses, the right to a jury trial, and the right to not testify against oneself. State State prosecutions follow the criminal procedure code of the individual state. Although every state has its own criminal procedure code, many states choose to mimic the Federal Rules. State procedural rules may offer greater protection to a defendant in a criminal trial than the U.S. Constitution or the Federal Rules, but may not offer less protection than guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution. Investigatory and Accusatory Police Procedure The U.S. Constitution, the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, state and local rules, and court interpretation of these documents not only set out how trials are run but also prescribe the procedures that law enforcement agencies must follow. Should an officer fail to abide by the proper procedure, the trial court may suppress evidence obtained in violation of proper procedure, which could even lead to the suspect's acquittal. Law enforcement agencies are limited in their abilities well before an arrest is made.
